meta.title: Who really said "Never let a good crisis go to waste"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Churchill — the attribution is a post-2008 backfill. The line is a popular compression of Rahm Emanuel's November 2008 remark, itself preceded by economist Paul Romer in 2004. The Saul Alinsky credit is a misattribution too.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Never let a good crisis go to waste'?
meta.ogDescription: Rahm Emanuel, 2008 — 'You never want a serious crisis to go to waste.' Not Churchill, and not Alinsky either: that credit is itself unsourced.

answer.label: Not Churchill — a compression of Rahm Emanuel (2008)
answer.authorDates: b. 1959 · American politician; White House chief of staff, 2009–2010
answer.sourceLine: Speaking to the Wall Street Journal CEO Council on 19 November 2008, Emanuel said: “You never want a serious crisis to go to waste. And what I mean by that is it’s an opportunity to do things that you think you could not do before.” The snappier imperative in circulation is a later compression — not a verbatim quotation of him or anyone else. The Churchill credit appeared only after 2008.

source.excerpt: You never want a serious crisis to go to waste. And what I mean by that is it's an opportunity to do things that you think you could not do before.
trail: Emanuel’s remark to the Wall Street Journal CEO Council on 19 November 2008 is the nearest documented original, and he later clarified publicly what he had meant by it sourced wording ↗.
The immediate antecedent is the economist Paul Romer, who said in November 2004 that ‘a crisis is a terrible thing to waste’ — the thought, in a different sentence, four years earlier Romer ↗.

The Churchill attribution fails the basic test: the phrase appears nowhere in his speeches, books or papers, and the credit surfaces only after Emanuel’s 2008 remark made the idea famous — a textbook internet backfill onto a quote magnet Churchill Society red herrings ↗.
source.excerptNote: Emanuel’s actual sentence, with the explanation he gave in the same breath. Note it is a statement of fact, not the brisk command the compressed version turns it into.
source.rightsNote: The words themselves are free. A phrase this short is not protectable by copyright in the United States, Emanuel’s remark was extemporaneous speech, and there is no estate or rights holder to clear. The live issue is trademark, not copyright: the phrase is heavily used commercially as book and course titles, so check for conflicts before putting it on a product. And do not credit it to Churchill on anything you sell — that adds a false-attribution problem to a phrase that was otherwise free. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Winston Churchill
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Churchill
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British prime minister, statesman & Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Sir Winston Churchill led Britain through the Second World War and won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature. Any brisk, worldly line about adversity tends to drift toward him, and this one drifted a long way: it did not exist in his lifetime. The credit only appears after a serving American chief of staff said something similar in 2008 — a modern remark aged backwards by seventy years to borrow his authority.

copyAttribution: You never want a serious crisis to go to waste. —Rahm Emanuel, WSJ CEO Council, 19 November 2008. The compressed "never let a good crisis go to waste" is not verbatim, and is not Churchill's.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This line collects false credits the way few others do — Churchill, Alinsky, sometimes Machiavelli. Two of those three are worth correcting individually, because the second one is a misattribution that fact-checkers themselves keep repeating.

items.why: Absent from his speeches, books and papers, and unattested in his lifetime. The Churchill credit appears only after Emanuel’s 2008 remark circulated — the phrase was aged backwards to acquire gravitas red herrings ↗.

People who know it is not Churchill often credit Alinsky’s Rules for Radicals (1971). That is loose at best: Alinsky wrote that ‘in the arena of action a threat or crisis becomes almost a precondition to communication’ — thematically adjacent, not this sentence. Do not swap one unsourced credit for another.

Emanuel said ‘You never want a serious crisis to go to waste,’ a description. The imperative ‘never let a good crisis go to waste’ — sharper, and more cynical — is a later popular compression that is verbatim to no one his actual words ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Not Churchill and not Alinsky. The nearest real source is Rahm Emanuel on 19 November 2008, preceded by Paul Romer in 2004; the familiar imperative is a compression of Emanuel’s sentence sourced wording ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Emanuel meant it descriptively — a crisis suspends the usual objections, so things that were politically impossible become possible. Compressed into an imperative and stripped of his follow-on sentence, it reads instead as an instruction to exploit disaster, which is why it is now used almost entirely as an accusation.

That shift is the whole reason the Churchill credit stuck. Attach a cynical maxim to a wartime statesman and it sounds like hard-won realism; leave it with a serving political operative and it sounds like an admission.
detailsBody: Paul Romer, November 2004: ‘A crisis is a terrible thing to waste.’
Rahm Emanuel, 19 November 2008: ‘You never want a serious crisis to go to waste… it’s an opportunity to do things that you think you could not do before.’
After 2008: compressed to the imperative ‘never let a good crisis go to waste.’
Later still: credited variously to Churchill, Alinsky and Machiavelli — none of them sourced.
context.pull: The phrase did not exist in Churchill's lifetime.
